title: Childhood incident asthma and traffic-related air pollution at home and school.
ehr_evidence: Parent-reported physician diagnosis of new-onset asthma (n = 120) was identified during 3 years of follow-up of a cohort of 2,497 kindergarten and first-grade children who were asthma- and wheezing-free at study entry into the Southern California Children's Health Study; exposure was estimated from a line source dispersion model and regional O3, NO2, PM10, and PM2.5 measured continuously at one central site monitor in each of 13 communities.
summary: In a prospective longitudinal cohort of 2,497 kindergarten and first-grade children in Southern California, modeled traffic-related pollution exposure at home and school and regional ambient pollutants were associated with increased risk of new-onset asthma.
key_findings: Nonfreeway traffic-related pollution (TRP) at home was associated with increased new-onset asthma risk (HR 1.51; 95% CI, 1.25–1.82; p < 0.001).
Nonfreeway TRP at school was associated with increased risk (HR 1.45; 95% CI, 1.06–1.98).
Combined time-weighted home and school nonfreeway TRP exposure had a stronger association (HR 1.61; 95% CI, 1.29–2.00).
Ambient NO2 measured at a community central site was associated with more than double the risk of new-onset asthma (HR 2.17; 95% CI, 1.18–4.00; p = 0.01).

In models co-adjusting for NO2 and modeled traffic exposures, associations of asthma with home (HR 1.46) and school (HR 1.45) TRP remained independent, whereas the NO2 estimate was attenuated (HR 1.37; 95% CI, 0.69–2.71).
Freeway TRP and PM10, PM2.5, and O3 were not significantly associated with new-onset asthma.
There were no significant interactions of residential or school nonfreeway TRP with sex, allergy, or parental history of asthma.
captured_features: Modeled nonfreeway, freeway, and total traffic-related pollution (TRP) at home and school
Distance to nearest freeway/highway/arterial road and traffic volume within 150 m of home and school
Meteorology (wind speed, wind direction, mixing layer height)
Ambient central-site NO2, O3, PM10, and PM2.5
Parent-reported physician diagnosis of new-onset asthma
Age, sex, race/ethnicity, secondhand smoke, wildfire smoke, health insurance, housing, allergy history, parental asthma, maternal smoking, pets, income, parental education
population: 2,497 kindergarten and first-grade children (ages ~4.8–9.0 years) asthma- and wheezing-free at baseline, from 45 schools in 13 Southern California communities
exposure_domain: Traffic-related air pollution (NO2, PM, O3, traffic volume, proximity, meteorology)
limitations: Conservative TRP estimates for the center of school buildings likely underestimate true student exposure, especially during dropoff/pickup.
Retrospective questionnaire assessment of early-life risk factors (not a pregnancy cohort).
Asthma has no sensitive/specific diagnostic test; parent-reported physician diagnosis may introduce misclassification.
Selection bias from loss to follow-up and exclusion of children who left the community or had asthma/wheeze at entry.
